2	name: reference-posthog-admin-access
3	description: PostHog personal API key for the Agenta Cloud project (US, project 34631) lives in ~/.agenta-posthog.env; scoped to that project, feature-flag write; the wallet rollout flags live there
4	metadata:

6	---
7	
8	`~/.agenta-posthog.env` (chmod 600) holds `POSTHOG_PERSONAL_API_KEY`, `POSTHOG_HOST=https://us.posthog.com`, and the project name. The key is scoped to one project: use project-based endpoints only (`/api/projects/34631/...` or `/api/projects/@current/...`); `/api/projects/` itself returns permission_denied.
9	
10	Project 34631 "Agenta Cloud". Payload flags follow one shape: active, one group at 100% rollout, payload stored as a JSON string under `filters.payloads["true"]` (see `starter-credits-bridge-policy`, `blocked-domains`).
11	
12	Wallet rollout flags (created 2026-10-02, empty so they affect nobody): `llm-gateway-rollout` (id 928418, payload `[]`, list of org ids) and `wallets-rollout` (id 928419, payload `{}`, org id -> off/shadow/enforce). The API reads them only with `AGENTA_ROLLOUT_FLAGS_ENABLED=true`. Changing a payload is a production rollout action: only on Mahmoud's go. See [[project-wallets-takeover]].
13

1	---
2	name: project-cloud-runs-on-gcp-not-aws
3	description: HARD FACT 2026-10-15 - Agenta cloud (live EU+US and the preview stages) runs on GCP/GKE, not AWS; never reach for aws sso, rds_connect or ec2_connect
4	metadata:
5	  type: project
6	---
7	
8	Agenta cloud runs on GCP now. Mahmoud corrected me on 2026-10-15 after I asked him to run `aws sso login` to look up a customer's Stripe customer id: "we are using gcp now, we are not working aws anymore."
9	
10	**Why:** the AWS notes ([[agenta-cloud-debug-access]], [[project_agenta_cloud_deploy]]) predate the GKE cutover and sent me to dead tooling.
11	
12	**How to apply:** for any production lookup, use gcloud, not aws. Never suggest `aws sso login`, `rds_connect.sh` or `ec2_connect.sh`.
13	
14	Production layout (from agenta_cloud `hosting/kubernetes/gcp/`, origin/main, 2026-10-15):
15	- GCP project `agenta-prod`. Account `mahmoud@agenta.ai`. If gcloud says "Reauthentication failed", Mahmoud must run `gcloud auth login` himself (interactive).
16	- live-eu: cluster `agenta-prod-eu`, region europe-west3, kube context `gke_agenta-prod_europe-west3_agenta-prod-eu`, namespace `live-eu`, Cloud SQL `agenta-prod-eu-pg-live`, Secret Manager `agenta-prod-eu-live-app-env`, host eu.cloud.agenta.ai.
17	- live-us: cluster `agenta-prod-us`, region us-east4, kube context `gke_agenta-prod_us-east4_agenta-prod-us`, namespace `live-us`, Cloud SQL `agenta-prod-us-pg-live`, Secret Manager `agenta-prod-us-live-app-env`, host us.cloud.agenta.ai.
18	- Postgres is Cloud SQL on a private IP with TLS, so reach it from inside the cluster (kubectl exec into an api pod), not from the dev box.
19	- Admin calls: read AGENTA_AUTH_KEY from the app-env secret in a script (never print it), then `Authorization: Access <key>` on /api/admin/... routes.
20	- Preview stages: [[reference-gcp-stage-qa-access]]. Deploy: agenta_cloud workflow 29 (`29-deploy-to-gke.yml`). Infra Terraform: agenta-infra `environments/gcp/*`.
21	
22	Working recipe (verified 2026-10-15):
23	- Read-only SQL: `kubectl --context <ctx> -n live-<region> exec -i deploy/agenta-api -c api -- sh -c 'PGSSLMODE=require psql "$(echo $POSTGRES_URI_CORE | sed -e "s#+asyncpg##" -e "s#?.*##")" -f -' < query.sql`. psql rejects the URI's `?ssl=` param, hence the sed.
24	- Stripe portal link for an org: same exec, `curl -s -X POST "http://localhost:8000/admin/billing/stripe/portals/?organization_id=<id>" -H "Authorization: Access $AGENTA_AUTH_KEY"`. The key stays inside the pod.
25	- If the gcloud token is stale, start `gcloud auth login mahmoud@agenta.ai --no-launch-browser` in the app's Terminal panel on the dev box; Mahmoud types the password there. A login on another machine does not reach the dev box.
26

<system-reminder>This memory is 121 days old. Memories are point-in-time observations, not live state — claims about code behavior or file:line citations may be outdated. Verify against current code before asserting as fact.</system-reminder>
1	---
2	name: project_codex_subscription_pi
3	description: "How Pi uses the OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex subscription (no API key) end to end, the capability-table bug fixed, and the live sidecar topology"
4	metadata: 
5	  node_type: memory
6	  type: project
7	  originSessionId: 1596f6f1-0fdb-44e9-b97b-3860c4b1b6b8
8	---
9	
10	Feature: run Pi on the OpenAI **ChatGPT/Codex subscription** (OAuth) instead of an `OPENAI_API_KEY`.
11	
12	**How to configure an agent for it:** harness `pi_core`/`pi_agenta`, model under provider `openai-codex` (all 4 Pi 0.79.4 codex models verified working on the subscription: `gpt-5.5` / `gpt-5.4` / `gpt-5.4-mini` / `gpt-5.3-codex-spark`; wire = `openai-codex/<id>`), connection `mode: self_managed`.
13	
14	**Why `openai-codex` not `openai`:** Pi has two distinct providers. `openai` = api.openai.com, `openai-responses`/`completions` API, `OPENAI_API_KEY`. `openai-codex` = chatgpt.com/backend-api, `openai-codex-responses` API, ChatGPT OAuth. The provider id selects endpoint+protocol+which auth.json credential. `self_managed` only means "use my own login", not which OpenAI endpoint (a self-managed OpenAI could be a BYO API key OR the subscription), so the provider id is load-bearing. Could add a friendly UI label ("OpenAI (ChatGPT subscription)") but cannot collapse to one `openai`.
15	
16	**Setup skill:** `.agents/skills/subscription-sidecar/` (dual-login Claude + codex recipe, wiring, verification). `self_managed` short-circuits the vault → `credentialMode: runtime_provided`, empty `secrets` → runner falls back to Pi's OAuth login. Even a project WITH an OpenAI key uses the subscription under `self_managed` (short-circuit runs before the vault). In `agenta` (default) mode it only uses the subscription if NO openai key is set (tolerant fallback to runtime_provided); with a key present it injects the key (API, not subscription).
17	
18	**Pi auth fact:** the subscription login lives in Pi's own `~/.pi/agent/auth.json` (provider key `openai-codex`, from `pi` then `/login` → ChatGPT). NOT the Codex CLI's `~/.codex/auth.json`. There is NO standalone codex harness — codex is a Pi provider. `~/.pi/agent/settings.json` defaults `defaultProvider: openai` / `gpt-4o-mini`, so bare `pi` CLI errors "No API key found for openai"; the runner's `pickModel` normalizes any `gpt-5.x` onto `openai-codex` so /run works.
19	
20	**Bug fixed (2026-06-30):** `sdks/python/agenta/sdk/agents/capabilities.py` `PI_VAULT_PROVIDERS` omitted `openai-codex`, so the agent service `_check_harness_pre_resolve` → `harness_allows_provider("pi_core","openai-codex")` raised `UnsupportedProviderError` BEFORE the run reached the runner — app-layer dead even though the runner handles codex fine. Fix = new `PI_SUBSCRIPTION_PROVIDERS=["openai-codex"]` + `PI_SUBSCRIPTION_MODELS` added to `providers` and `_pi_models()` for pi_core/pi_agenta. Tests: `test_capabilities.py` + new `test_pi_openai_codex_self_managed_reaches_session` in services `test_invoke_handler.py`. Matrix doc updated. NOT committed (local working tree).
21	
22	**Live topology (EE wp-b2-rendering stack, :8280):** services + API set `AGENTA_AGENT_RUNNER_URL=http://agenta-claude-sub-sidecar:8765` — the app routes to the **ad-hoc** `agenta-claude-sub-sidecar`, NOT the compose `sandbox-agent`. I recreated that sidecar to mount BOTH subscription logins: `~/.claude:ro` (Claude) + `~/.pi/agent` copied to a writable `/home/agent/.pi/agent` (codex); runs as uid 1000 (= host mahmoud), no `OPENAI_API_KEY`. Orig config snapshot saved to the session scratchpad. The compose `sandbox-agent` (runs as root, `~/.pi/agent:ro`→copy `/pi-agent`) also has fresh codex auth but the app does not use it.
23	
24	**Gotcha:** SDK edits need a **services AND api container restart** — both mount `sdks/python → /sdks/python` but uvicorn reload only watches `/app`. See [[project_subscription_sidecar_stale_no_hotreload]], [[project_agent_workflows_qa]], [[reference_harness_config_models]].
25

/** Which attempt a poll addresses: an attempt is polled through its own connection. */
export interface LoginAttemptKey {
    secretId: string
    attemptId: string
    /** When the poll started, so the backstop can stop a server that answers `pending` forever. */
    startedAt: number
    /** Whose connection it is; an organization login is polled with its scope. */
    scope?: SecretOwnerScope
}

// A string, because `atomFamily` dedupes by value: an object would make a poll per render.
export const loginAttemptKey = ({secretId, attemptId, startedAt, scope}: LoginAttemptKey): string =>
    [secretId, attemptId, startedAt, ...(scope === "organization" ? [scope] : [])].join("|")

const parseLoginAttemptKey = (serialized: string): LoginAttemptKey | null => {
    const [secretId, attemptId, startedAt, scope] = serialized.split("|")
    if (!secretId || !attemptId) return null
    return {
        secretId,
        attemptId,
        startedAt: Number(startedAt) || 0,
        ...(scope === "organization" ? {scope} : {}),
    }
}

/** The next interval, or `false` to stop. Outside the query options so it is testable. */
export const loginAttemptPollInterval = ({
    state,
    pollAfterMs,
    startedAt,
    now = Date.now(),
}: {
    state?: string | null
    pollAfterMs?: number | null
    startedAt?: number
    now?: number
}): number | false => {
    if (isTerminalLoginAttemptState(state)) return false
    if (startedAt && now - startedAt > LOGIN_ATTEMPT_BACKSTOP_MS) return false
    return Math.max(pollAfterMs ?? MIN_LOGIN_POLL_MS, MIN_LOGIN_POLL_MS)
}

// Only a 404 says the attempt is gone; every other failure leaves it redeemable, so keep polling.
const attemptIsGone = (error: unknown): boolean =>
    (error as {response?: {status?: number}} | null)?.response?.status === 404

// What a card should DO, on the same backstop the poll stops on. `unreadable` wins: it recovers.
export type LoginAttemptOutcome = "waiting" | "succeeded" | "failed" | "unreadable" | "timed_out"

export const loginAttemptOutcome = ({
    state,
    error = null,
    startedAt,
    now = Date.now(),
}: {
    state?: string | null
    /** What the last poll threw, if it threw. Only a 404 ends the attempt. */
    error?: unknown
    startedAt?: number
    now?: number
}): LoginAttemptOutcome => {
    if (attemptIsGone(error)) return "unreadable"
    if (state === "succeeded") return "succeeded"
    if (isTerminalLoginAttemptState(state)) return "failed"
    if (startedAt && now - startedAt >= LOGIN_ATTEMPT_BACKSTOP_MS) return "timed_out"

"""Device login and login upkeep for a hosted subscription connection.

Three callers meet here. The browser starts, polls, and cancels a device login. The runner
pod that runs a device login's provider poll reports how it ended. A run pushes a refreshed
login back after a turn, and reports a login that stopped working. All of them edit the
same subscription secret, so every decision that reads the stored login is made against
the locked row (`VaultService.update_secret_atomically`).

The attempt record on the row is the only state a poll reads. The runner pods behind the
Service URL are interchangeable, so a poll must not depend on reaching the one pod that
holds the provider poll in memory.
"""

from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from typing import Any, Dict, Optional
from uuid import UUID

from pydantic import BaseModel

from oss.src.core.secrets.dtos import (
    SecretResponseDTO,
    SubscriptionLoginAttemptDTO,
    SubscriptionProviderDTO,
    UpdateSecretDTO,
    UpdateSecretPayloadDTO,
)
from oss.src.core.secrets.claude_token import ClaudeTokenClient
from oss.src.core.secrets.enums import (
    SUBSCRIPTION_PROVIDER_DISPLAY_NAMES,
    SecretKind,
    SubscriptionLoginState,
    SubscriptionProviderKind,
)
from oss.src.core.secrets.services import VaultService
from oss.src.core.secrets.subscription_login import (
    RunnerLoginAttempt,
    SubscriptionLoginRunnerClient,
)
from oss.src.core.secrets.subscription_rules import (
    PushDecision,
    attempt_is_live,
    classify_push,
    failure_is_stale,
    login_is_usable,
    parse_attempt_deadline,
    push_reason,
)
from oss.src.core.secrets.types import (
    SubscriptionLoginAttemptNotFound,
    SubscriptionProviderMismatch,
    SubscriptionSecretNotFound,
    SubscriptionTokenRejected,
)
from oss.src.utils.logging import get_module_logger


log = get_module_logger(__name__)

_PENDING = "pending"
_SUCCEEDED = "succeeded"

# A reason string comes from the runner and is shown to the user, so it is bounded.
_MAX_LOGIN_ERROR_LENGTH = 200

_INVALID_LOGIN_REASON = "invalid_login"

# Every token `claude setup-token` prints starts with this.
_CLAUDE_TOKEN_PREFIX = "sk-ant-oat"

# The reason the runner gives when the provider's device-code window runs out.
_TIMED_OUT_REASON = "timed_out"

# How long past the provider's deadline a pending record waits before a poll calls it
# expired. The runner reports the provider's last answer at about the deadline, and its
# retries take at most 27 s (`OUTCOME_REPORT_RETRY_DELAYS_MS` and
# `OUTCOME_REPORT_TIMEOUT_MS` in `services/runner/src/subscription-login-attempts.ts`), so a
# success at the deadline still finds its record. Keep this grace above that sum.
_DEADLINE_GRACE = timedelta(seconds=30)

# Push decisions worth a warning rather than an info line.
_WARNED_PUSH_DECISIONS = {PushDecision.INVALID, PushDecision.OTHER_ACCOUNT}


class SubscriptionLoginAttemptView(BaseModel):
    """What a browser learns about an in-flight device login. Never the credential."""

    attempt_id: str
    state: str
    user_code: Optional[str] = None
    verification_uri: Optional[str] = None
    expires_at: Optional[str] = None
    poll_after_ms: Optional[int] = None
    error: Optional[str] = None


class SubscriptionLoginPushResult(BaseModel):
    version: int
    generation: int
    updated: bool
    stale: bool = False
    # The current login, sent back only on a stale answer, so the runner can rematerialize
    # without a second call.
    login: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None
    # Why a push was not stored, as a stable slug. `same_login` means the row already holds
    # this exact credential, which is the one refusal that still tells the runner its
    # credential is current; every other slug (`invalid_login`, `older_login`,
    # `other_account`, `wrong_generation`, `no_login`) means the row kept something else.
    # An accepted push and a stale answer carry none: `updated` and `stale` say it.
    reason: Optional[str] = None


class SubscriptionLoginFailureResult(BaseModel):
    stale: bool
    version: int
    generation: int
    login: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None


def _log_attempt(
    secret_id: UUID,
    attempt_id: str,
    state: str,
    outcome: str,
    *,
    warn: bool = False,
) -> None:
    """One line per attempt decision. Never the user code, never the credential.

    `connection` is the key the runner uses for the same id, so one query follows a sign-in
    across the hop.
    """
    write = log.warning if warn else log.info
    write(
        "subscription.attempt",
        connection=str(secret_id),
        attempt_id=attempt_id,
        state=state,
        outcome=outcome,
    )


def _log_push(
    secret_id: UUID,
    stored: SubscriptionProviderDTO,
    generation: int,
    decision: PushDecision,
) -> None:
    """One line per push decision. Never the credential.

    Two decisions warn, because both mean a run pushed something that cannot belong here: an
    unusable credential, and a login for another ChatGPT account. The ordering refusals are
    the protocol working, so they stay at info.
    """
    write = log.warning if decision in _WARNED_PUSH_DECISIONS else log.info
    write(
        "subscription.push",
        connection=str(secret_id),
        incoming_generation=generation,
        stored_generation=stored.login_generation,
        stored_version=stored.login_version,
        decision=decision.value,
    )


def _log_failure(
    secret_id: UUID,
    stored: SubscriptionProviderDTO,
    stale: bool,
    reason: str,
) -> None:
    log.info(
        "subscription.failure",
        connection=str(secret_id),
        stored_generation=stored.login_generation,
        stored_version=stored.login_version,
        stale=stale,
        reason=_clip(reason),
    )


def _subscription_data(secret: SecretResponseDTO) -> SubscriptionProviderDTO:
    data = secret.data
    if not isinstance(data, SubscriptionProviderDTO):
        raise SubscriptionSecretNotFound()
    return data


def _update_with(secret: SecretResponseDTO, changes: Dict[str, Any]) -> UpdateSecretDTO:
    """An update carrying the WHOLE stored payload plus `changes`.

    Every field is stated, so the keep-on-omit carry-over has nothing to fill in and an
    explicit clear (a finished attempt, a cleared error) survives the write.
    """
    data = _subscription_data(secret).model_dump(mode="json")
    data.update(changes)

    return UpdateSecretDTO(
        secret=UpdateSecretPayloadDTO(
            kind=SecretKind.SUBSCRIPTION_PROVIDER,
            data=data,

# Onboarding questions and the signup survey: one vocabulary

Last updated: 2026-10-27.

The first-agent onboarding and the EE post-signup survey ("Signup 3 - Agents" in PostHog)
both ask who the person is. They used different option lists and different property names,
so the same person produced two answers that could not be counted together. This page is the
mapping that makes them one.

## Who writes what

| Property | Shape | Written by | Values |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `user_role_v2` | string | onboarding; the survey only with `$set_once` while it still asks role | the role labels below |
| `company_size_v2` | string | onboarding; the survey only with `$set_once` while it still asks size | Solo, 2-10, 11-50, 51-200, 201+ |
| `referral_source_v2` | string | onboarding only | the source labels below |
| `agent_experience_v2` | string | the survey | Not yet — just exploring, Built prototypes or side projects, Running some in production, Running many at scale |
| `is_icp_v2` | boolean | nobody from now on; older persons keep the survey's value | derived in reporting, see below |

One writer per topic. The onboarding owns role, size and source. The survey keeps agent
experience, intent and the email backfill. PostHog person properties are last-write-wins and
keep no history, so a second writer would make "who said this" unanswerable. Until the survey
stops asking role and size, it writes them with `$set_once`: it fills them for someone who
never saw the onboarding and never replaces an onboarding answer. Its referral answer is a
list, so it stays on the `survey sent` event and is not written to `referral_source_v2`.

`is_icp_v2` needs company size, role and agent experience, which now arrive from two surfaces.
No form writes it any more. A value stored before this change can disagree with the current
inputs, so reporting derives the current result instead (see below).

## Role: old label to new chip

Counts are persons on the Agenta Cloud project on 2026-10-27.

| Old label | People | New chip |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hobbyist — personal projects | 353 | Hobbyist |
| Software Engineer | 236 | Engineer (AI, SWE, ML) |
| Freelancer / Consultant / Agency | 135 | Freelancer / Consultant / Agency (unchanged) |
| Founder or Executive | 129 | Founder or Executive (unchanged) |
| AI/ML Engineer or Data Scientist | 95 | Engineer (AI, SWE, ML) |
| Product Manager | 83 | Product Manager (unchanged) |
| Ops / Automation (BizOps, RevOps, IT) | 69 | IT / Operations |
| Engineering (one stray value) | 1 | Engineer (AI, SWE, ML) |

New buckets with no history: Sales, Marketing, Support, Student, Other.

The two unchanged labels are deliberately unchanged. Identical strings are what let an answer
from before the switch sit in the same bucket as an answer after it. Renaming one splits the
history and buys nothing.

Chips, in order, with the catalog category each puts first under the gallery's Recommended

* preference, the middleware does this before anything renders. Pass `enabled: false` while a
 * sign-in is still in flight; see the `/auth` note below for why that matters.
 *
 * `route` is the host router's path, a dependency only: sign-in and post-signup leave by a
 * client-side push from pages this hook must skip, so without it the hop never re-runs.
 *
 * `location.replace`, not the router: `/m` is a different Next app behind the same origin, so
 * this is a document navigation whichever way it is spelled — and replace keeps the desktop URL
 * out of history, where Back would bounce off it.
 *
 * DELIBERATELY ONE-WAY. `/m` must not grow a mirror of this hook. The two apps are separate JS
 * contexts sharing only storage, so each would redirect on a value the other cannot see, with
 * nothing to arbitrate and nothing to break the cycle: any disagreement becomes an endless
 * `/w` ↔ `/m` bounce instead of a stop. Leaving `/m` is the proxy's job — one cookie, and the
 * desktop gate yields to it through `wantsClassic`.
 */
export const useClassicModeRedirect = (
    enabled = true,
    route?: string,
    /** Host hook to amend the `/m` target just before leaving; must be a stable function. */
    prepareTarget?: (target: string) => string,
) => {
    const userId = useAtomValue(activeUserIdAtom)
    const advancedNavHidden = useSettledAdvancedNavHidden()

    useEffect(() => {
        if (!enabled || typeof window === "undefined") return
        // No user means no preference to read, and `null` means it is not known yet. Redirecting
        // on either is a navigation this effect cannot take back.
        if (!userId || !advancedNavHidden) return

        const {pathname, search} = window.location
        // Never from `/auth`, even though the gate maps it: post-auth sets the user id and the
        // signup-era default and THEN routes onward, so a user is briefly known while still
        // standing on the sign-in page. Redirecting into that window races the router and, for a
        // new EE user, skips the post-signup survey outright.
        if (/^\/auth(\/|$)/.test(pathname)) return
        if (isDesktopOnlyLink(pathname, search)) return
        if (readCookie(MOBILE_OPTOUT_COOKIE)) return

        const target = mobileRouteFor(pathname, search)
        if (!target) return
        // Publish before navigating, exactly as the Classic mode switch does. Relying on the
        // sync effect above having already run makes this correct only by hook order; if the
        // cookie is missing when `/m` is asked for, its proxy sees no preference, falls through
        // to the device check, and bounces a desktop UA straight back here. That is a loop.
        writeClassicModeCookie(false)
        window.location.replace(prepareTarget ? prepareTarget(target) : target)
    }, [enabled, userId, advancedNavHidden, route, prepareTarget])
}

/**
 * `/m`-only: the desktop page matching wherever the user is standing, for the Classic mode
 * switch to send them to. Falls back to the desktop root.
 */
export const desktopEscapeHref = (): string => {
    if (typeof window === "undefined") return "/w"
    // The address bar carries `/m`; the route map works in basePath-less paths.
    const {pathname, search} = window.location
    const stripped = pathname === "/m" ? "/" : pathname.replace(/^\/m(?=\/)/, "")
    return desktopRouteFor(stripped, search) ?? "/w"
}

/**
 * An `/auth` link carrying `auth_error` completes on desktop, for the same reason as a token: the
 * param IS the payload. `web/oss/src/lib/api/assets/axiosConfig.ts` redirects a 403 here so the
 * user can finish required SSO or social re-authentication, and the desktop auth page reads it.
 * `mapDesktopToMobile` returns a bare `/m/auth`, so redirecting would drop the reason and leave
 * the user on a sign-in screen that cannot explain why it appeared.
 */
export function isPolicyAuthLink(pathname: string, search: string): boolean {
    if (!AUTH_RE.test(pathname)) return false
    return Boolean(new URLSearchParams(search).get("auth_error"))
}

const DESKTOP_EXCEPTIONS = [AUTH_CALLBACK_RE, /^\/post-signup(\/|$)/, /^\/workspaces\/accept(\/|$)/]

/**
 * Routes that finish where they landed, whatever any gate would prefer: an OAuth callback, the
 * post-signup survey, an invite acceptance, and any `/auth` link carrying a one-time token or a
 * policy error. One list, so the middleware and the client-side redirect cannot disagree.
 */
export function isDesktopOnlyLink(pathname: string, search: string): boolean {
    if (DESKTOP_EXCEPTIONS.some((re) => re.test(pathname))) return true
    return isTokenBearingAuthLink(pathname, search) || isPolicyAuthLink(pathname, search)
}

/**
 * Desktop sub-paths under `/apps` that are NOT an agent id — they must not be read as one.
 * `/apps/archived` is the archived list, `/apps/agent-templates` the template gallery.

const APPS_RESERVED = new Set(["archived", "agent-templates"])

/** Strips leading and trailing `/`. A loop, not a regex: `/\/+$/` backtracks on long `/` runs. */
const trimSlashes = (value: string) => {
    let start = 0
    let end = value.length
    while (start < end && value[start] === "/") start++
    while (end > start && value[end - 1] === "/") end--
    return value.slice(start, end)
}

/** `?template=<key>` when the URL carries a website template link, else "". */
const templateQueryFrom = (search: string): string => {
    const templateKey = new URLSearchParams(search).get(TEMPLATE_QUERY_PARAM)?.trim()
    return templateKey ? `?${TEMPLATE_QUERY_PARAM}=${encodeURIComponent(templateKey)}` : ""
}

Links: [{"title":"What version of Codex is running?","url":"https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/9418"},{"title":"What happened","url":"https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/22810"},{"title":"What is the type of issue?","url":"https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/9327"},{"title":"codex cli workspace disabled","url":"https://www.betterclaw.io/tools/agent-error-decoder/codex-cli-workspace-disabled"},{"title":"codex device code auth chatgpt security 2026","url":"https://lucaberton.com/blog/codex-device-code-auth-chatgpt-security-2026/"},{"title":"# Codex Headless Login: Device Code, SSH Tunnel, or auth.json","url":"https://blog.laozhang.ai/en/posts/codex-headless-login.md"},{"title":"codex headless login","url":"https://blog.laozhang.ai/en/posts/codex-headless-login"}]

The search found no official OpenAI page on this error. The results are mostly user reports and third-party blogs, so treat the details as unverified.

- **Cause:** Users who hit the "contact your workspace admin" message were on Business or Enterprise workspaces where device code login was disabled. One GitHub reporter said they were the workspace admin and still couldn't find the setting ([GitHub issue #9327](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/9327)). In that case a member can't enable it alone ([laozhang](https://blog.laozhang.ai/en/posts/codex-headless-login)).
- **Where the setting is:** An OpenAI team member reportedly pointed to chatgpt.com/#settings/Security for personal accounts and chatgpt.com/admin/permissions for workspace admins ([laozhang](https://blog.laozhang.ai/en/posts/codex-headless-login)). The label is reportedly "Enable Codex Device Code Authorization" under Settings → Security, but that comes from user reports, not official docs ([laozhang](https://blog.laozhang.ai/en/posts/codex-headless-login)).
- **Related error:** A different message, `codex_cli_workspace_disabled`, appears when an admin has Codex turned off for the workspace or a user's role excludes it. A third-party site recommends asking an admin to enable local Codex use in workspace settings ([BetterClaw](https://www.betterclaw.io/tools/agent-error-decoder/codex-cli-workspace-disabled)).
- **Fallbacks:** If device code stays blocked, one option is an SSH tunnel on port 1455 or copying `auth.json` from a machine that is already signed in ([laozhang](https://blog.laozhang.ai/en/posts/codex-headless-login-device-code)). The source for that tip is a different laozhang page from the one above.

The most useful step is to have a workspace admin check the device code setting in the admin permissions page and confirm the user's role includes Codex. If that fails, OpenAI support at help.openai.com is the escalation path.

+/**
+ * SuperTokens' cookie-mode session cookies that reach a page request (both on path `/`). Either
+ * one means a session exists; the gate never validates it, the app does that after it loads.
+ */
+const SESSION_COOKIES = ["sAccessToken", "sFrontToken"]
+
+/**
+ * Where a signed-out visitor with no Classic mode preference signs in, or `null` to stay.
+ *
+ * Only the entry points move: bare `/w` (where `/` redirects) and `/auth`. A deep link keeps the
+ * desktop sign-in, which returns the user to it (`?redirectToPath=`); `/m`'s sign-in always lands
+ * on its home screen. A website template link goes to the `/m` root, which keeps the key across
+ * sign-in; `/m/auth` would drop it.
+ */
+const signedOutEntryRoute = (pathname: string, search: string): string | null => {
+    if (/^\/w\/?$/.test(pathname)) {
+        const templateQuery = templateQueryFrom(search)
+        return templateQuery ? `/m/${templateQuery}` : "/m/auth"
+    }
+    if (AUTH_RE.test(pathname) && !new URLSearchParams(search).has("redirectToPath")) {
+        return "/m/auth"
+    }
+    return null

content.text:
I found the cause of the missing survey. For the ChatGPT login, I know what happened but not yet why, because the auto mode permission check blocked my production read.

## 1. ChatGPT login

**What happened to Asma (session replay, times in UTC):**

| Time | What happened |
|---|---|
| 10:42:44 | Asma clicked Connect. Agenta returned a code and the link `auth.openai.com/codex/device`. |
| 10:42:52 to 10:43:52 | Asma copied the code three times and left the tab between copies. |
| Until 10:45:51 | Each check returned HTTP 200, and the page stayed on "Waiting for you to sign in". |
| 10:45:51 | Asma made a click with no text on the target, probably closing the dialog. |
| 10:45:52 | Asma clicked Continue. |

Asma later created an agent, and that run produced traces. I did not check which connection it ran on.

**What this tells us:**
- **The start of the login worked:** Agenta got a code from OpenAI, so the first step is fine.
- **The sign-in never finished:** the page never showed a success or an error message. Either the problem was on the OpenAI page, or our side never received the result.
- **Asma may not have used our link:** PostHog recorded no click on "Open ChatGPT". A middle-click or a typed address would also not appear, so this is not proof.
- **It may not be only Asma:** one other real user (`sadikkedir02@gmail.com`) tried on 2026-10-29. That user waited about 5 minutes, clicked "Open ChatGPT", copied the code again and left. The replay shows no success.

**Most likely cause (not proven):** OpenAI's device code sign-in may be turned off for the account.
- User reports say this setting is off by default for personal accounts, and that a workspace admin controls it for Business accounts. I found no official OpenAI page that confirms this.
- Asma's company has 51-200 people, so a workspace account is possible.
- Our dialog does not mention this setting, and any error would appear only on the OpenAI page.

**What would settle it:** the `subscription.attempt` log lines and the stored row for connection `01a18c67-a4a9-78f0-b9b1-8acf96257dc4`, attempt `b4ee3018-0f1e-43d2-aee6-b57b12167560`. They show whether OpenAI declined the login, the code expired, or our side lost the result. This is the access the box above asks for.

## 2. Survey

**Asma's answers are not lost.** They are in PostHog as person properties, sent with `onboarding_step_completed`: Marketing, 51-200, Friend or colleague.

**The `survey sent` event no longer fires for most new signups:**
- Commit `6d4f0bf42c`, in v0.127.2, sends signed-out visitors from `/w` and `/auth` to `/m/auth`.
- The survey exists only on `/post-signup` in the old app, and the `/m` sign-in never goes there.
- The last `survey sent` event was at 08:47 UTC today. The three signups since then have none, and two of them went through the new onboarding. The third, `comicdoge47@gmail.com`, has no onboarding events either.
- Only sign-in links with `redirectToPath` still use the old sign-in page.

**What we lose with the survey:**
- **Agent experience (`agent_experience_v2`):** nothing else writes it. Our ICP (ideal customer) definition requires this answer, so new signups can no longer count as ICP.
- **The intent answer:** the new onboarding does not ask this.
- **The email backfill:** the survey wrote this too, and the new onboarding does not.
- **`first_agent_intent`:** this event may also stop for new users on `/m`. Asma has none, although `web/mobile` still has a helper for it. I did not finish tracing this one.

**Decision needed:** the survey change looks like a side effect of the routing fix, not a choice to drop those answers. I recommend adding one "agent experience" question to the `/m` onboarding, using the labels the survey already has. That keeps the ICP number working and adds one click. Bringing back the old survey page would mean a second form and a detour out of `/m`. Accepting the loss would mean redefining ICP without that answer.

Sources: [openai/codex #9327](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/9327), [openai/codex #9418](https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/9418), [Codex headless login guide](https://blog.laozhang.ai/en/posts/codex-headless-login)

content.text:
The logs show that Agenta's login flow worked correctly for this attempt, but OpenAI never gave our runner a login for it. **The failure happened before or at the OpenAI approval step.** I still can't say exactly why Asma's approval did not complete, because OpenAI's page does not report back to us.

**Timeline from the EU logs (UTC):**

| Time | Log entry | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 10:42:46 | `state=pending`, `outcome=started` | The API and the runner started the attempt. |
| 10:42:46 to 10:45:51 | `GET .../login-attempts/...` returned 200 | The browser checked the status while Asma was on the page. |
| 10:45:52 | No log entry; this time comes from the replay | Asma clicked Continue, and the attempt kept running. |
| 10:57:46 | `state=expired`, `report=delivered status=204` | OpenAI's 15-minute window ran out, and the runner reported this to the API. |

**What this rules out:**
- **Lost result:** the runner's report reached the API, and the attempt was not abandoned on a pod.
- **Crash or restart:** the same runner pod started and ended the attempt.
- **Declined login or other error:** the attempt ended as `expired`, so OpenAI did not send an error that stopped our polling.

**What is still open:** there are two possible explanations, and our logs can't separate them.
1. **Asma never completed the approval on OpenAI's page (most likely).** The device code setting I mentioned earlier could explain this, and so could a confusing page or an unsuitable account. OpenAI shows any such error only on its own page.
2. **OpenAI refused our runner's status checks.** The Pi library treats HTTP 403 and 404 as "still waiting" (`pi-ai/dist/utils/oauth/openai-codex.js:204`). If OpenAI blocked those checks, even an approved login would look the same as this one. I think this is less likely, because the same runner got the code from OpenAI without a problem. The logs do not record these HTTP responses, so I can't exclude it.

**Separate product gaps:**
- **No guidance in the dialog:** it says nothing about the device code setting and gives no help if OpenAI's page refuses the code.
- **No visible failure:** Asma would have seen the "code expired" message only by keeping the dialog open for 15 minutes. Asma had already moved on and got no message.
- **Closing the dialog does not stop the attempt:** the attempt ran for another 12 minutes after Asma continued. This did no harm.

**What I did not read:** I did not read the database row. The logs answered the question, and the row holds the encrypted login data.

**Next step:** I want to count how all recent ChatGPT logins ended in EU and US, using only the state words in the logs (`succeeded`, `expired`, `failed`), with no user data. If some succeed, the problem is specific to certain accounts and better guidance in the dialog is the fix. If none succeed, the login is broken for everyone and explanation 2 becomes the main suspect. Your approval covered only this one attempt, so the box above asks for this wider read.

The survey decision from my last message is still open. I still recommend adding the "agent experience" question to the `/m` onboarding.

Base directory for this skill: /home/mahmoud/.claude/skills/communicating-with-mahmoud

# Communicating with Mahmoud

Doing the work is half the job, and communicating it is the other half. Mahmoud reads the
chat to make decisions, so a correct result written up as a data dump is a failure. He has
said more than once that he would switch models over output he cannot read. Treat every
writeup as part of the deliverable.

For sentence style, load `~/.claude/skills/plain-writing/SKILL.md` and follow it. This
skill adds the rules about the reader, the structure, and the process.

## The reader

- Mahmoud is a senior Python developer and architect. He is a beginner in TypeScript and
  frontend work. Explain frontend ideas in terms he can map from the backend.
- He did not read the PR. He does not know the shorthand you built up this session, and he
  does not care in which order you found things.
- For docs, the reader is a stranger with a job, not a teammate. Never assume what they
  know. Phrases such as "the part teams get wrong" or "the first question people ask" are
  banned.

## Structure: context first, then a story

Use this order:

1. Context. What the thing is and why it exists. A reader with no session context must be
   able to follow from here.
2. The choices or parts, one at a time. For each one: how it works, what the user installs
   or does, where things live, and the trade-off.
3. How they combine, with a concrete live example.
4. Limits and gaps.
5. The plan or the options, with a recommendation.

Apply these rules across the whole piece:

- Give each section one axis. Pick the reader's natural questions ("how does it run
  locally?", "what do I install?", "what breaks?") and answer them in order. Do not spread
  one topic across three sections.
- Write headings as plain signposts that state the content. A heading is not a sentence and
  not a clever label.
- Explain how things work today before you describe a change. Show before and after with
  concrete examples: real data shapes and real code.
- If an explanation is short and complicated, rewrite it long and simple.
- Give every decision its reasoning: the problem, the options, the trade-offs, the choice,
  and why. "We do X" with no reason is a review comment waiting to happen.

## Banned patterns

These rules are absolute. Repeat them in every subagent brief.

- No em dashes. Use a period and a new sentence, parentheses, or a semicolon. Check the
  places where they come back: term definitions, trade-off lists, asides, and list item
  separators. The count must be zero.
- No slang: soak, bikeshed, yak-shaving, greenfield, and similar words. Say the plain thing,
  for example "after it has run in real use for a while without problems".
- No drama: "precise and damning", "the one that bit you", "say the word", cute closing
  lines, narrative tension. Debugging and status updates are flat: what happened, what it
  means, what is next.
- No undefined terms. Define every term on first use (runner, vault, sandbox, harness,
  overlay, and any other domain term).
- No bare internal labels. Never use a code such as F-7, C2, Tier 1 or P0 without restating
  it in plain words, every time. He does not remember labels between messages. Prefer names
  that describe themselves, such as "must fix before enabling".
- No meta text in the body. Never write "amended after review", "added per finding", or
  "updated per X" in a doc or report. Provenance goes in PR comments or an appendix.
- Use bold and bullets only when they help quick reading. A wall of bullets should be prose.

## Two lists: what I do, what you do

Always separate "what I will do" from "what you need to do" as two explicit lists. Do not
mix your actions and his actions in one paragraph.

## When he is tired or confused

Drop all compression. Use short sentences with one idea each, numbered steps, and say who
does what at each step. A status update in the middle of the work follows the same rules.

## Questions

- In strategy, brainstorm, and thinking-out-loud conversations, ask one open prose question
  at a time. Do not use multi-select menus. If options help, mention them inline as
  suggestions.
- Use structured multiple choice only for a real, discrete fork in execution work.

## Verify before you assert

- Never write an instruction or claim you have not checked against the code, the config
  file, or the actual behavior. Fluent, confident, wrong instructions cost the reader hours.
  If you cannot verify a claim, cut it.
- Before you hand over docs, run an adversarial pass: a fresh check whose job is to find
  what is still wrong against this skill and `plain-writing`. A self-assessment is not
  evidence.

## Subagent output is your output

- Read everything a subagent wrote (PR body, design doc, report) against this skill before
  you tell Mahmoud it is ready. A rewrite round after he reads it counts as a failure.
- Naming this skill in a brief is not enough. Copy the reader profile and the banned
  patterns above into the brief, word for word.

## PR descriptions

The `write-pr-description` skill, when the repo has it, holds the full procedure. These
rules always apply:

1. Lead with the concrete symptom: what was broken, from the user's point of view.
2. Then the fix in plain words, with a concrete before and after. Show the real data shapes
   when a transformation changed.
3. Then a short section on tests and notes.
4. Add a "How to review" section that walks the diff in reading order.
5. Leave inline comments on the subtle hunks to explain the reason a reviewer would
   otherwise have to work out.

Cut vague bullets that restate the diff, checkbox theater, and "Summary" boilerplate. The
title states the actual change, for example
`fix(api): map OpenInference tool definitions into real tool objects`.

Base directory for this skill: /home/mahmoud/.claude/skills/plain-writing

# Plain writing

The plain writing skill captures how the user wants writing to read: plain,
boring, and easy to understand in one pass. Apply it by default when you write
for them.

There are four groups of rules: word choice and tone, sentences and paragraphs,
punctuation and formatting, and patterns to avoid. Each rule has a before and
after. After the rules comes the deslopify command.

## Word choice and tone

1. **Use simple, everyday words.** Don't pick a fancy synonym when a plain word
   works. Also avoid words AI tools overuse, e.g., "delve", "tapestry",
   "landscape", "robust", "leverage", and "reach".
   Before: We leverage the cache to unlock a more robust query experience.
   After: We use the cache to make repeated queries faster.

2. **No jargon.** Always use human-understandable language, the way two people
   talk to each other. Don't invent jargon or shorthand (that is, if a word or
   phrase is not in the Merriam Webster dictionary, don't use it). Use
   established technical terms only when they are most precise, and briefly
   define them when readers may not know them.
   Before: The score is a calibrated proxy for whether the property holds.
   After: The score estimates how likely the property is to hold.

3. **No puffery or empty emphasis.** Drop words that add emphasis but no
   information, e.g., "really", "real", "matters", "worth", "carries weight",
   "boasts", "a testament to", "pivotal", "renowned", and "quietly". State the
   actual point, or cut the sentence.
   Before: This result matters, and it carries weight for the design.
   After: The scores barely moved, so we can skip the model on most documents.

4. **Use consistent terminology and constrain your vocabulary.**
   Before: Upload the document. The file is parsed, and the record is saved.
   After: Upload the document. The document is parsed and saved.

5. **It's ok to use contractions.** They match everyday speech, so use them
   freely.
   Before: Do not worry, it is not going to overwrite your file.
   After: Don't worry, it's not going to overwrite your file.

6. **Do not invent hyphenated adjectives.** Avoid a phrase you make up by
   joining words with a hyphen to sound compact or clever. If you would not find
   it in a dictionary, don't use it. A common compound adjective that people
   already use is fine, e.g., "well-crafted".
   Before: We added a reveal-style colon to the output.
   After: We added a colon that shows the schema.

7. **Keep the writing boring, descriptive, and explanatory.** Do not use a
   catchy phrase, slogan, clever label, or wording meant to sound memorable.
   This rule applies everywhere; to headings, topic sentences, callouts,
   labels, summaries, and ordinary prose.
   Before: Legal requirements as a floor.
   After: Applicable legal constraints.
   Before: # The alignment loop
   After: # Iterative refinement using development disagreements

## Sentences and paragraphs

8. **Write complete sentences.** Each sentence should have a subject and a
   verb. Do not write fragments, and do not stitch unrelated ideas together with
   colons or semicolons. But it is ok to join closely related ideas with plain
   conjunctions, like "and", "because", or "so".
   Before: The agent polls the file and reacts to changes, and the team meets on
   Tuesdays.
   After: The agent polls the file and reacts to changes. The team meets on
   Tuesdays.

9. **When you present a workflow or sequence, walk through it in order.** Use
   "First", "Second", "Third", and give each step its own sentence so the
   reader can follow it, or break up steps with semicolons.
   Before: The groups the features were sorted into were the authors' own
   reading, the example posts were written by hand, and finer detail meant
   training extra small models and labeling again.
   After: First, the authors sorted the features into groups themselves, based on
   their own reading of the outputs. Second, they wrote the example posts by
   hand. Third, when they wanted finer detail, they trained another small
   model, and they labeled the posts again.

10. **Organize a paragraph as a topic sentence and then support.** Start each
   paragraph or section with a topic sentence that states the main point. Then,
   the next sentence should be a supporting example or fact, with an extra
   sentence about it if it needs one. Then, introduce more support with a plain
   connective like "For example", "Moreover", or "Or".
   Before: The parser skips files with no changes. The cache holds the previous
   output. Most renders are fast.
   After: Most renders are fast. For example, the parser skips files with no
   changes, so the server returns early. Moreover, the cache keeps the previous
   output, so a repeated render does no work.

11. **Never write three or more clauses in one sentence, or three or more
    example sentences in a row.** In ordinary prose, a sentence may have one or
    two related clauses. Do not pack three or more clauses into one prose
    sentence. If you need that many points, use a numbered First / Second / Third
    sequence under rule 9, or short bullet points when you are writing a
    brief. If list points are examples and you want to inline them, introduce
    with "e.g.". Also do not give three or more example sentences back to back
    to support the same point.
    Before: The parser reads the file, the validator checks the fields, and the
    writer saves the record.
    After: The parser reads the file, and the validator checks the fields. The
    writer then saves the record.

12. **Prefer long, explanatory sentences over short, punchy ones.** In ordinary
    prose, write the way people explain things out loud: longer sentences with
    commas, and the simplest way to say the point. Do not break one thought into
    a stack of short sentences, and don't write catchy short phrases. Short
    lines are fine only in labeled briefs, bullets, or a First / Second / Third
    sequence, e.g., "To do: validate recall on long queries."
    Before: The gate runs on every merge. It blocks regressions. Nobody
    bypasses it.
    After: The gate runs on every merge, and it blocks changes that fail a
    regression case. A regression cannot make it to production, unless someone
    deliberately overrides the check.
    Before: Search ranking now uses a scored model instead of heuristics. The
    change reduced p95 latency from 900 ms to 220 ms. We still need to validate
    recall on long queries.
    After: Search ranking now uses a scored model instead of heuristics, and
    p95 latency fell from 900 ms to 220 ms. To do: validate recall on long
    queries.

13. **Be precise and unambiguous, and cut unnecessary clauses.** Say exactly
    what changes, who does what, or by what mechanism. Prefer a concrete
    statement over an evocative abstraction, e.g., don't say things like
    "improvement stops being guesswork". Also drop trailing or side clauses
    that add no fact, e.g., "before we call the work done", "as we move
    forward", or "for the time being". Keep the sentence long when the content
    needs it, but do not pad it.
    Before: With trusted scores, improvement stops being guesswork.
    After: With trusted scores, you can measure whether each change helped,
    so you keep or revert each change based on the measured result.
    Before: We still need to validate recall on long queries before we call
    the work done.
    After: To do: validate recall on long queries.

14. **In chat, give context on the problem.** When you are chatting back and
    forth, write for a smart reader who does not have context on the problem,
    or who forgot it. Give context on the problem and on what was happening
    before. Then say what changed. Keep the setup short. Do not dump the whole
    history. Ignore this rule if you are writing an essay.
    Before: The exporter now waits on the reset header, and `dotnet test` is
    green.
    After: The Okta System Log exporter was rereading whole hours, so a retry
    could write the same event twice. It now waits using the response reset
    header, and the six acceptance tests pass.

## Punctuation and formatting

15. **No dashes or middle dots.** Do not use em dashes or en dashes, including in
    number ranges. Join clauses with a period or "and", and write ranges with
    "to". Do not use the middle dot (·) as a separator; use a comma, "and", or
    separate lines instead.
    Before: The build is fast — it finishes in 10 to 20 seconds.
    After: The build is fast. It finishes in 10 to 20 seconds.

16. **Don't use colons to join clauses in ordinary prose.** Do not use a colon
    to glue two clauses or to set up a point in essay-like writing. A colon is
    fine when you introduce a list. A colon is also fine as a short label in
    updates, briefs, status notes, and PR descriptions, e.g., "Summary:",
    "Changes:", or "Remaining work:".
    Before: Read for the schema: the feature fires.
    After: Read for the schema. The feature fires.
    Before (allowed in a PR or update): Summary: Replace em dashes in
    generated docs.
    After (same text is fine): Summary: Replace em dashes in generated docs.

17. **Use straight quotes, not curly quotes.**
    Before: The system logs each “event” as it happens.
    After: The system logs each "event" as it happens.

18. **Keep the formatting plain.** Use sentence case in headings. Do not use
    bold for decoration.
    Before: ## How To Install The Skill
    After: ## How to install the skill

19. **You can use lists, but do not overuse them.** Keep a list to three or
    four points, and nest extra points if you need more. When you are writing
    an essay, use lists and tables very sparingly.
    Before: Shipped this week:
    - dark mode
    - an invite link fix
    - a schema mismatch that blocked analytics export
    - renderer cleanup
    - copy edits
    - a scored ranking model
    - a p95 drop from 900 ms to 220 ms
    - untested recall on long queries
    After: Search ranking now uses a scored model, and p95 latency fell from
    900 ms to 220 ms. The old heuristic path is still in the repo as a
    fallback.
    - Shipped
      - Dark mode
      - Invite link fix
    - Still open
      - Test recall on long queries
      - Unblock analytics export

## Patterns to avoid

20. **Do not give inanimate things fake agency.** Do not write as if a system
    or object transforms, decides, or intends on its own when a person or
    process is the real actor. Ordinary factual verbs for tools and systems are
    fine, e.g., "The API returns JSON", "The job writes the file", or "The
    paper argues". Prefer a human or process subject when that is clearer.
    Before: The logs become searchable records, once the job finishes.
    After: You can search the logs, once the job finishes.

21. **No analogies or imagery.** Do not explain by comparing to something else,
    and do not use metaphor. Describe the actual thing in literal terms. Write
    in a boring way.
    Before: The feature index is like a card catalog that the optimizer can flip
    through.
    After: The feature index is a list of named features. The optimizer can look
    up which feature matches a request.

22. **Never use negative parallelism of the form "not just X, it is Y" or
    "not only X, but Y".** State what the thing is. A plain refusal or
    correction is fine, including a short quote of a customer's hype phrase
    when you replace it with a concrete fact.
    Before: It is not just a parser, it is a full toolchain.
    After: It is a parser and a formatter.
    Before: We do not describe the API as "enterprise-grade robust," because
    that phrase can mean different things.
    After: The API has a 99.9% monthly uptime SLO.

23. **Do not stack rhetorical questions.** AI writing often asks two or three
    rhetorical questions in a row to sound thoughtful. Don't do this. Just state
    the problem directly.
    Before: Does the tool keep the writer's voice? Does it make the argument
    stronger or weaker?
    After: We do not yet know whether the tool keeps the writer's voice, or
    whether it makes the argument stronger or weaker.

24. **Do not use vague demonstrative pronouns.** Do not use "This", "That",
    "These", or "Those", especially do not start a sentence with a demonstrative
    pronoun, and never begin a paragraph with a sentence that contains a
    demonstrative anywhere in it.
    Before: That context carries into the next turn.
    After: The agent applies the rules you saved on the next turn.

25. **Do not open with a count of things.** Never start by announcing how many
    points are coming, e.g., "Two cautions." or "Three things to keep in mind."
    State the first point directly. If you absolutely must present many things,
    use a bullet list instead.
    Before: Two cautions. First, the section can drift out of date. Second,
    it can balloon if every item gets a sentence.
    After: The section can drift out of date, because it duplicates facts
    that live elsewhere. It can also balloon if every item gets a sentence.

## The deslopify command

When the user says `/plain-writing deslopify`, rewrite the previous agent
response, or the text after the command, for a sharp CEO or technical reader
who has no project context. Return only the rewrite.

Start with the main conclusion, then cover the background, how it works, and
present all information logically and sequentially. Include technical details
the reader needs (standardize on existing well-known terminology, not new
terminology), and define unfamiliar terms.

Follow the plain-writing rules above.
